{{nihongo|'''Wabi-sabi'''|[[wikt:侘|侘]][[wikt:寂|寂]]}} represents a comprehensive [[Japan]]ese [[world view]] or [[aesthetic]] centered on the acceptance of [[wikt:transience|transience]] and imperfection. The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete".<ref name=Koren/> It is a concept derived from the [[Buddhist]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, the other two being {{nihongo|[[dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.
Characteristics of the wabi-sabi aesthetic include [[asymmetry]], [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] (roughness or irregularity), simplicity, economy, austerity, modesty, intimacy and appreciation of the ingenuous integrity of natural objects and processes.
==Description== "Wabi-sabi is the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of traditional Japanese beauty and it occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese [[wiktionary:pantheon|pantheon]] of aesthetic values as do the [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[beauty]] and perfection in the West".<ref name=Koren/> "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be wabi-sabi."<ref name=Juniper>{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2003 | isbn=0-8048-3482-2}}</ref> "[Wabi-sabi] nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name=Powell>{{cite book | author=Powell, Richard R. | title=Wabi Sabi Simple | publisher=Adams Media | year=2004 | isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
The words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' do not translate easily. ''Wabi'' originally referred to the loneliness of living in nature, remote from society; ''sabi'' meant "chill", "lean" or "withered". Around the 14th century these meanings began to change, taking on more positive connotations.<ref name=Koren>{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> ''Wabi'' now connotes rustic simplicity, freshness or quietness, and can be applied to both natural and human-made objects, or understated elegance. It can also refer to quirks and anomalies arising from the process of construction, which add uniqueness and elegance to the object. ''Sabi'' is beauty or serenity that comes with age, when the life of the object and its impermanence are evidenced in its patina and wear, or in any visible repairs.
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, wabi-sabi eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' shifted to become more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to [[satori]], or enlightenment. In today's Japan, the meaning of wabi-sabi is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity." In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), pp. 20–21.</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref>
A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.

Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]

[[File:RyoanJi-Dry garden.jpg|thumb|[[Zen garden]] of [[Ryōan-ji]]. It was built during the [[Higashiyama period]]]] [[Image:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|right|A Japanese tea house which reflects the wabi-sabi aesthetic in [[Kenroku-en]] (兼六園) Garden]] [[Image:Black Raku Tea Bowl.jpg|thumb|right|Wabi-sabi tea bowl, [[Azuchi-Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
{{nihongo|'''Wabi-sabi'''|[[wikt:侘|侘]][[wikt:寂|寂]]}} represents a comprehensive [[Japan]]ese [[world view]] or [[aesthetic]] centered on the acceptance of [[wikt:transience|transience]] and imperfection. The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete".<ref name=Koren/> It is a concept derived from the [[Buddhist]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, the other two being {{nihongo|[[dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.
Characteristics of the wabi-sabi aesthetic include [[asymmetry]], [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] (roughness or irregularity), simplicity, economy, austerity, modesty, intimacy and appreciation of the ingenuous integrity of natural objects and processes.
==Description== "Wabi-sabi is the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of traditional Japanese beauty and it occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese [[wiktionary:pantheon|pantheon]] of aesthetic values as do the [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[beauty]] and perfection in the West".<ref name=Koren/> "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be wabi-sabi."<ref name=Juniper>{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2003 | isbn=0-8048-3482-2}}</ref> "[Wabi-sabi] nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name=Powell>{{cite book | author=Powell, Richard R. | title=Wabi Sabi Simple | publisher=Adams Media | year=2004 | isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
The words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' do not translate easily. ''Wabi'' originally referred to the loneliness of living in nature, remote from society; ''sabi'' meant "chill", "lean" or "withered". Around the 14th century these meanings began to change, taking on more positive connotations.<ref name=Koren>{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> ''Wabi'' now connotes rustic simplicity, freshness or quietness, and can be applied to both natural and human-made objects, or understated elegance. It can also refer to quirks and anomalies arising from the process of construction, which add uniqueness and elegance to the object. ''Sabi'' is beauty or serenity that comes with age, when the life of the object and its impermanence are evidenced in its patina and wear, or in any visible repairs.
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, wabi-sabi eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' shifted to become more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to [[satori]], or enlightenment. In today's Japan, the meaning of wabi-sabi is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity." In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), pp. 20–21.</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref>
A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>
==See also== * [[Clinamen]] * [[Higashiyama Bunka]] in [[Muromachi period]] * [[iki (aesthetic ideal)|Iki]] (a Japanese aesthetic ideal) * [[Mono no aware]] * [[Shibui]] * [[Teaism]] * [[Wabi-cha]]
==References== {{reflist|2}}
* {{cite book | author=Crowley, James and Sandra | title=Wabi Sabi Style | publisher=Gibbs Smith, Publisher | year=2001 | isbn=1-58685-753-3}} * {{cite book | author=Suzuki, Daisetz T. | title=Zen and Japanese Culture | chapter=Chapter 2: General Remarks on Japanese Art Culture | publisher=MJF Books | location= New York | year=1959 | pages=19–38 | isbn=1-56731-124-5}} * Tierney, Lennox (1999), ''Wabi Sabi'', Layton, Utah: Gibbs Smith, Publisher. ISBN 0-87905-849-8
==External links== * [http://nobleharbor.com/tea/chado/WhatIsWabi-Sabi.htm "What Is Wabi-Sabi?".] Essay by [[Tadao Ando]] * [[WikiWikiWeb:WabiSabi|Wabi-sabi influence]] on [[Wiki]] and [[extreme programming]]

From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref>
A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>
In 2013, in a critically acclaimed blog post featured on [http://wordpress.com/fresh/ Freshly Pressed], [http://about.me/chaitanya_chunduri Chaitanya Chunduri] - a prolific marketing blogger at [http://brandednoise.com/ BrandedNoise], coined the term '''[http://brandednoise.com/2013/07/28/the-wabi-sabi-edge/ The Wabi Sabi Edge]'''. The concept draws inspiration from varied sources like the [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in Japan, the yearly [[Burning_man|Burning Man]] event and the theory of [http://hbr.org/2013/06/transient-advantage/ar/1 Transient Advantage] in Business strategy. His idea posits the following: "Essentially from which ever perspective you look at it – artistic, personal, emotional, professional or even strategic, the ability to accept transience as the new normal, the ability to let go of the status quo to rethink, re-invent and renew our approach forms the bedrock of the new competitive edge – The Wabi Sabi Edge."<ref>http://brandednoise.com/2013/07/28/the-wabi-sabi-edge/</ref>

Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>

[[File:RyoanJi-Dry garden.jpg|thumb|[[Zen garden]] of [[Ryōan-ji]]. It was built during the [[Higashiyama period]]]] [[Image:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|right|A Japanese tea house which reflects the wabi-sabi aesthetic in [[Kenroku-en]] (兼六園) Garden]] [[Image:Black Raku Tea Bowl.jpg|thumb|right|Wabi-sabi tea bowl, [[Azuchi-Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
{{nihongo|'''Wabi-sabi'''|[[wikt:侘|侘]][[wikt:寂|寂]]}} represents a comprehensive [[Japan]]ese [[world view]] or [[aesthetic]] centered on the acceptance of [[wikt:transience|transience]] and imperfection. The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete".<ref name=Koren/> It is a concept derived from the [[Buddhist]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, the other two being {{nihongo|[[dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.
Characteristics of the wabi-sabi aesthetic include [[asymmetry]], [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] (roughness or irregularity), simplicity, economy, austerity, modesty, intimacy and appreciation of the ingenuous integrity of natural objects and processes.
==Description== "Wabi-sabi is the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of traditional Japanese beauty and it occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese [[wiktionary:pantheon|pantheon]] of aesthetic values as do the [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[beauty]] and perfection in the West".<ref name=Koren/> "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be wabi-sabi."<ref name=Juniper>{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2003 | isbn=0-8048-3482-2}}</ref> "[Wabi-sabi] nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name=Powell>{{cite book | author=Powell, Richard R. | title=Wabi Sabi Simple | publisher=Adams Media | year=2004 | isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
The words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' do not translate easily. ''Wabi'' originally referred to the loneliness of living in nature, remote from society; ''sabi'' meant "chill", "lean" or "withered". Around the 14th century these meanings began to change, taking on more positive connotations.<ref name=Koren>{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> ''Wabi'' now connotes rustic simplicity, freshness or quietness, and can be applied to both natural and human-made objects, or understated elegance. It can also refer to quirks and anomalies arising from the process of construction, which add uniqueness and elegance to the object. ''Sabi'' is beauty or serenity that comes with age, when the life of the object and its impermanence are evidenced in its patina and wear, or in any visible repairs.
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, wabi-sabi eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' shifted to become more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to [[satori]], or enlightenment. In today's Japan, the meaning of wabi-sabi is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity." In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), pp. 20–21.</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref>
A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>
==See also== * [[Clinamen]] * [[Higashiyama Bunka]] in [[Muromachi period]] * [[iki (aesthetic ideal)|Iki]] (a Japanese aesthetic ideal) * [[Mono no aware]] * [[Shibui]] * [[Teaism]] * [[Wabi-cha]]

It was built during the [[Higashiyama period]]]] [[Image:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|right|A Japanese tea house which reflects the wabi-sabi aesthetic in [[Kenroku-en]] (兼六園) Garden]] [[Image:Black Raku Tea Bowl.jpg|thumb|right|Wabi-sabi tea bowl, [[Azuchi-Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
{{nihongo|'''Wabi-sabi'''|[[wikt:侘|侘]][[wikt:寂|寂]]}} represents a comprehensive [[Japan]]ese [[world view]] or [[aesthetic]] centered on the acceptance of [[wikt:transience|transience]] and imperfection. The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete".<ref name=Koren/> It is a concept derived from the [[Buddhist]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, the other two being {{nihongo|[[dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.
Characteristics of the wabi-sabi aesthetic include [[asymmetry]], [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] (roughness or irregularity), simplicity, economy, austerity, modesty, intimacy and appreciation of the ingenuous integrity of natural objects and processes.
==Description== "Wabi-sabi is the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of traditional Japanese beauty and it occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese [[wiktionary:pantheon|pantheon]] of aesthetic values as do the [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[beauty]] and perfection in the West".<ref name=Koren/> "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be wabi-sabi."<ref name=Juniper>{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2003 | isbn=0-8048-3482-2}}</ref> "[Wabi-sabi] nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name=Powell>{{cite book | author=Powell, Richard R. | title=Wabi Sabi Simple | publisher=Adams Media | year=2004 | isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
The words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' do not translate easily. ''Wabi'' originally referred to the loneliness of living in nature, remote from society; ''sabi'' meant "chill", "lean" or "withered". Around the 14th century these meanings began to change, taking on more positive connotations.<ref name=Koren>{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> ''Wabi'' now connotes rustic simplicity, freshness or quietness, and can be applied to both natural and human-made objects, or understated elegance. It can also refer to quirks and anomalies arising from the process of construction, which add uniqueness and elegance to the object. ''Sabi'' is beauty or serenity that comes with age, when the life of the object and its impermanence are evidenced in its patina and wear, or in any visible repairs.
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, wabi-sabi eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' shifted to become more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to [[satori]], or enlightenment. In today's Japan, the meaning of wabi-sabi is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity." In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), pp. 20–21.</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary wabi-sabi tea bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the wabi-sabi style]] A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Here is an incomplete list: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>

Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary wabi-sabi tea bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the wabi-sabi style]] A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Examples include: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>
Potter [[Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques and founded an influential European aesthetic movement which also included Dame [[Lucy Rie]] and [[Hans Coper]].
Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux traveled throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people, beginning by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living Wabi Sabi'' by [[Taro Gold]] to "ask people on a Tokyo street to describe Wabi Sabi." Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>
In the hills of Asheville, NC, musician/artist/philosopher, Rusty Douglas began applying the Wabi-Sabi principles to his custom guitar work to create one of a kind instruments that reflect the beautiful imperfections that occur when nature runs its course. " Rusty combines painting, pottery, woodwork, geology, the culinary arts and story-telling to create a new/old kind of instrument."<ref>barnyard-guitars.com</ref>

''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>

[[File:RyoanJi-Dry garden.jpg|thumb|[[Zen garden]] of [[Ryōan-ji]]. It was built during the [[Higashiyama period]]]] [[Image:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|right|A Japanese tea house which reflects the wabi-sabi aesthetic in [[Kenroku-en]] (兼六園) Garden]] [[Image:Black Raku Tea Bowl.jpg|thumb|right|Wabi-sabi tea bowl, [[Azuchi-Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
{{nihongo|'''Wabi-sabi'''|[[wikt:侘|侘]][[wikt:寂|寂]]}} represents a comprehensive [[Japan]]ese [[world view]] or [[aesthetic]] centered on the acceptance of [[wikt:transience|transience]] and imperfection. The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete".<ref name=Koren/> It is a concept derived from the [[Buddhist]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, the other two being {{nihongo|[[dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.
Characteristics of the wabi-sabi aesthetic include [[asymmetry]], [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] (roughness or irregularity), simplicity, economy, austerity, modesty, intimacy and appreciation of the ingenuous integrity of natural objects and processes.
==Description== "Wabi-sabi is the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of traditional Japanese beauty and it occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese [[wiktionary:pantheon|pantheon]] of aesthetic values as do the [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[beauty]] and perfection in the West".<ref name=Koren/> "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be wabi-sabi."<ref name=Juniper>{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence | publisher=Tuttle Publishing | year=2003 | isbn=0-8048-3482-2}}</ref> "[Wabi-sabi] nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name=Powell>{{cite book | author=Powell, Richard R. | title=Wabi Sabi Simple | publisher=Adams Media | year=2004 | isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
The words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' do not translate easily. ''Wabi'' originally referred to the loneliness of living in nature, remote from society; ''sabi'' meant "chill", "lean" or "withered". Around the 14th century these meanings began to change, taking on more positive connotations.<ref name=Koren>{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> ''Wabi'' now connotes rustic simplicity, freshness or quietness, and can be applied to both natural and human-made objects, or understated elegance. It can also refer to quirks and anomalies arising from the process of construction, which add uniqueness and elegance to the object. ''Sabi'' is beauty or serenity that comes with age, when the life of the object and its impermanence are evidenced in its patina and wear, or in any visible repairs.
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, wabi-sabi eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' shifted to become more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to [[satori]], or enlightenment. In today's Japan, the meaning of wabi-sabi is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity." In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), pp. 20–21.</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, ''wabi'' may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; then ''sabi'' could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word sabi, to rust. Specifically, although the Japanese kanji characters 錆 (''sabi'', meaning "rust") and 寂 (''sabi'', as above) are different, as are their applied meanings, yet the original spoken word (pre-kanji, ''yamato-kotoba'') is believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題,井上勝也,裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary wabi-sabi tea bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the wabi-sabi style]] A good example of this embodiment may be seen in certain styles of Japanese pottery. In the [[Japanese tea ceremony]], the pottery items used are often rustic and simple-looking, e.g. [[Hagi ware]], with shapes that are not quite symmetrical, and colors or textures that appear to emphasize an unrefined or simple style. In fact, it is up to the knowledge and observational ability of the participant to notice and discern the hidden signs of a truly excellent design or glaze (akin to the appearance of a diamond in the rough). This may be interpreted as a kind of wabi-sabi aesthetic, further confirmed by the way the colour of glazed items is known to change over time as hot water is repeatedly poured into them (''sabi'') and the fact that tea bowls are often deliberately chipped or nicked at the bottom (''wabi''), which serves as a kind of signature of the ''Hagi-yaki'' style.
''Wabi'' and ''sabi'' both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Mahayana philosophy itself, however, warns that genuine understanding cannot be achieved through words or language, so accepting wabi-sabi on nonverbal terms may be the most appropriate approach. Simon Brown <ref name="Brown">{{cite book | author=Brown, Simon | title=Practical Wabi Sabi | publisher=Carroll & Brown |year=2007 | isbn=1-904760-55-4}}</ref> notes that wabi-sabi describes a means whereby students can learn to live life through the senses and better engage in life as it happens, rather than be caught up in unnecessary thoughts. In this sense wabi-sabi is the material representation of Zen Buddhism. The idea is that being surrounded by natural, changing, unique objects helps us connect to our real world and escape potentially stressful distractions.
In one sense wabi-sabi is a training whereby the student of wabi-sabi learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. Wabi-sabi can change our perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}}
The ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' concepts are religious in origin, but actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual. The [[syncretic]] nature of Japanese belief systems should be noted.
==Wabi-sabi in Japanese arts== Many [[Japanese art]]s over the past thousand years have been influenced by [[Zen]] and [[Mahayana]] philosophy, particularly acceptance and contemplation of the imperfection, constant [[flux]] and [[impermanence]] of all things. Such arts can exemplify a wabi-sabi aesthetic. Examples include: * [[Honkyoku]] (traditional [[shakuhachi]] music of wandering Zen monks) * [[Ikebana]] (flower arrangement) * [[Japanese garden]]s, [[Zen garden]]s and [[bonsai]] (tray gardens) * [[Japanese poetry]], particularly [[haiku]] * [[Japanese pottery]], notably [[Hagi ware]] * [[Japanese tea ceremony]]
A contemporary Japanese appraisal of this concept is found in the influential essay ''[[In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
==Western use== Designer Leonard Koren (b. 1948) in 1994 published ''Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers''<ref name=Koren/> as an examination of wabi-sabi, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite web|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|publisher=New York Times|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>

Some [[haiku in English]] adapt the wabi-sabi aesthetic, with spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. ISBN 0671628372 p285</ref>
The work of American artist [[John Connell]] (born 1940) is centered on the idea of wabi.<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref>
Former [[Stuckist]] artist and [[remodernist film]]maker [[Jesse Richards]] (born 1975) employs it in nearly all of his work, along with [[mono no aware]].
During the 1990s the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[Agile programming]] and [[Wiki]] to describe acceptance of the state of ongoing imperfection that is the product of these methods.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wabi Sabi | url = http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi | accessdate = 2006-11-19 }}</ref>
On 16 March 2009, [[Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[BBC Four]] as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming. Theroux showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable." <ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[Andrews McMeel Publishing]], ISBN 0-7407-3960-3), p. 6.</ref>
The ''[[King of the Hill]]'' episode "The Son Also Roses" references Wabi-sabi.
[[Jack Dorsey]], the billionaire founder of [[Twitter]] and [[Square, Inc.|Square]] is known to evangelize the Wabi-sabi philosophy of design.<ref>{{cite web | title = The Many Sides of Jack Dorsey | url = http://www.wired.com/business/2012/06/ff_dorsey/ | first = Steven | last = Levy | date = June 22, 2012 | work = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | accessdate = 2013-05-24 }}</ref>
