[[en:Wabi-sabi]] {{wikidata link|Q1142664}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ar:وابي سابي]][[az:Vabi-sabi]][[ca:Wabi-sabi]][[commons:Category:Wabi-sabi (esthetic concept)]][[cs:Wabi-sabi]][[de:Wabi-Sabi]][[en:Wabi-sabi]][[eo:Vabi-sabio]][[es:Wabi-sabi]][[et:Wabi-sabi]][[eu:Wabi-sabi]][[fa:وابی-سابی]][[fi:Wabi-sabi]][[fr:Wabi-sabi]][[gl:Wabi-sabi]][[he:ואבי-סאבי]][[hu:Vabi-szabi]][[id:Wabi-sabi]][[it:Wabi-sabi]][[ja:わび・さび]][[ka:ვაბი-საბი]][[ko:와비·사비]][[lt:Vabi Sabi]][[ms:Wabi-sabi]][[nl:Wabi-sabi]][[pa:ਵਾਬੀ-ਸਾਬੀ]][[pl:Wabi-sabi]][[pt:Wabi-sabi]][[ro:Wabi]][[ru:Ваби-саби]][[sah:Ваби-саби]][[simple:Wabi-sabi]][[sr:Ваби-саби]][[sv:Wabi-sabi]][[tr:Wabi-sabi]][[uk:Вабі]][[vi:Wabi-sabi]][[zh_yue:侘寂]][[zh:侘寂]] {{Short description|Japanese aesthetic about beauty in imperfection}} {{distinguish|wasabi}} {{Italic title}} [[File:250201 Ryoan-ji Kyoto Japan06s3.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Zen garden|Zen garden]] of [[:en:Ryōan-ji|Ryōan-ji]]. It was built during the [[:en:Higashiyama period|Higashiyama period]]. The [[:en:Clay|Clay]] wall, which is stained by age with subtle brown and orange tones, reflects {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} principles, with the rock garden reflecting {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} principles.<ref>森神逍遥 『侘び然び幽玄のこころ』桜の花出版、2015th year Morigami Shouyo,"Wabi sabi yugen no kokoro : seiyo tetsugaku o koeru joi ishiki" (Japanese) {{ISBN|978-4-434-20142-4}}</ref>]] [[File:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|A Japanese tea house which reflects the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in {{nihongo|[[:en:Kenroku-en|Kenroku-en]]|兼六園}} Garden]] [[File:Black Raku tea bowl Amadera.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} tea bowl, [[:en:Azuchi–Momoyama period|Azuchi–Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
In traditional [[:en:Japanese aesthetics|Japanese aesthetics]], {{nihongo||侘び寂び|'''wabi-sabi'''}} is centered on the acceptance of and imperfection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Wabi-Sabi? |url=https://nobleharbor.com/tea/chado/WhatIsWabi-Sabi.htm |access-date=2017-07-13 |website=nobleharbor.com}}</ref> The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of appreciating beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete" in nature.<ref name="Koren2">{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> It is prevalent in many forms of Japanese art.<ref>{{Cite book |last=DAVIES |first=TREVOR |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/1032029879 |title=1001 IDEAS THAT CHANGED THE WAY WE THINK. |date=2018 |publisher=CASSELL ILLUSTRATED |isbn=978-1-78840-088-6 |location=[Place of publication not identified] |pages=293 |oclc=1032029879}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Zia |first=East Liberty |title=Wabi-Sabi: The Japanese Art of Finding the Beauty in Imperfections |url=https://www.carnegielibrary.org/staff-picks/wabi-sabi-the-japanese-art-of-finding-the-beauty-in-imperfections/ |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is a composite of two interrelated aesthetic concepts, {{nihongo|||wabi}} and {{nihongo|||sabi}}. According to the [[:en:Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]], {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be translated as "subdued, austere beauty," while {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} means "rustic [[:en:patina|patina]]."<ref>{{cite web |title=Japanese Aesthetics |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/japanese-aesthetics/ |accessdate=31 October 2022 |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is derived from the [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[:en:Three marks of existence|Three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, {{nihongo|[[:en:Dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[:en:Śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.<ref>Daisetz Suzuki "Zen and Japanese Culture" Iwanami Shoten, 1940 ISBN 978-4004000204 The stillness of the tea ceremony is wider than silence. Synonymous with awabi. (136 pages)</ref>
Characteristics of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetics and principles include [[:en:asymmetry|asymmetry]], roughness, [[:en:simplicity|simplicity]], economy, austerity, modesty, [[:en:intimacy|intimacy]], and the appreciation of both natural objects and the forces of nature.
==Description== {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can be described as "the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of what we think of as traditional Japanese beauty. It occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese of aesthetic values as do the [[:en:Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[:en:Beauty|Beauty]] and perfection in the West."<ref name="Koren2" /> Another description of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} by Andrew Juniper notes that, "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}."<ref name="Juniper2">{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |url=https://archive.org/details/wabisabijapanese00juni |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2003 |isbn=0-8048-3482-2 |url-access=registration}}</ref> For Richard Powell, "{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name="Powell2">{{cite book |author=Powell, Richard R. |title=Wabi Sabi Simple |publisher=Adams Media |year=2004 |isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
When it comes to thinking about an English definition or translation of the words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' Andrew Juniper explains that, "They have been used to express a vast range of ideas and emotions, and so their meanings are more open to personal interpretation than almost any other word in the Japanese vocabulary." Therefore, an attempt to directly translate ''wabi-sabi'' may take away from the ambiguity that is so important to understanding how the Japanese view it.<ref name="Juniper2" />
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} changed to be more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Satori|Satori]]}} or [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. In today's Japan, the meaning of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity". In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty".<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), pp. 20–21.</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} artworks often emphasize the process of making the piece and that it is ultimately incomplete.<ref name=":022">{{Cite journal |last=John |first=Joseph D. |date=2007 |title=Experience as Medium: John Dewey and a Traditional Japanese Aesthetic |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/224026 |journal=The Journal of Speculative Philosophy |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.2307/25670649 |issn=1527-9383 |jstor=25670649}}</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; in this instance, {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or the limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word {{nihongo3|{{lit|to rust}}|錆|sabi}}. Although the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] characters for "rust" are not the same as {{nihongo||寂|sabi}} in {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, the original spoken word (pre-kanji, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yamato-kotoba|Yamato-kotoba]]}}) are believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題, 井上勝也, 裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary_wabi-sabi_tea_bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} style]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[:en:Mahayana Buddhist|Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[:en:Transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Since Mahayana philosophy predicates that genuine understanding is reached through experience rather than words, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} may best be appreciated non-verbally.
Although the {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} concepts are religious in origin, actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual, in keeping with the [[:en:Syncretic|Syncretic]] nature of [[:en:Religion in Japan|Japanese belief]].
==Education== {{Essay-like|section|date=March 2024}} In one sense {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is a training whereby the student of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can change the student's perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.<ref>Yury Lobo, ''In the Wake of Basho: Bestiary in the Rock Garden'', Xlibris, 2017, 23*</ref>
[[File:Meimeian08n4592.jpg|thumb|Nijiriguchi entrance of a tea house]]
== History == Wabi-sabi has roots in ancient Chinese [[Taoism]] and [[:en:Zen|Zen]] Buddhism. It started to shape Japanese culture when the Zen priest [[:en:Murata Jukō|Murata Jukō]] (村田珠光, 1423–1502) modified the [[:en:Japanese tea ceremony|tea ceremony]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Reibstein |first=Mark |title=Wabi Sabi |publisher=Little, Brown |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-316-11825-5 |language=English}}</ref> He introduced simple, rough, wooden and clay instruments to replace the gold, jade, and porcelain of the Chinese style tea service that was popular at the time. About one hundred years later, the tea master [[:en:Sen no Rikyū|Sen no Rikyū]] (千利休, 1522 – April 21, 1591) introduced wabi-sabi to the royalty with his design of the [[:en:Chashitsu|teahouse]]. "He constructed a teahouse with a door so low that even the emperor would have to bow in order to enter, reminding everyone of the importance of humility before tradition, mystery, and spirit."<ref name=":1" />
== In Japanese arts == At first, something that exhibited wabi-sabi qualities could only be discovered; it could be "found in the simple dwellings of the farmers that dotted the landscape, epitomized in neglected stone lanterns overgrown with moss or in simple bowls and other household utensils used by the common folk."<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Teiji |first=Itoh |title=Wabi Sabi Suki: The Essence of Japanese Beauty |publisher=Mazda Motor Corporation |year=1993}}</ref> However, towards the end of the late medieval period, the ruling class began using these aesthetic values to intentionally create "tea ceremony utensils, handicrafts, tea ceremony rooms and cottages, homes, gardens, even food and sweets, and above all manners and etiquette."<ref name=":2" />
Many forms of [[:en:Japanese art|Japanese art]] have been influenced by Zen and Mahayana philosophy over the past thousand years, with the concepts of the acceptance and contemplation of imperfection, and constant [[:en:flux|flux]] and [[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]] of all things being particularly important to Japanese arts and [[:en:Culture of Japan|culture]].<ref name="Juniper2" /> Accordingly, many Japanese art forms can be seen to encapsulate and exemplify the ideals of ''wabi-sabi''.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Garden design === [[File:Kare-sansui zen garden, Ryōan-ji, Kyoto 20190416 1.jpg|thumb|Ryōan-ji (late 16th century) in Kyoto, Japan, a famous example of a Zen garden]] [[:en:Japanese garden|Japanese garden]]s started out as very simple open spaces that were meant to encourage kami, or spirits, to visit. During the Kamakura period Zen ideals began to influence the art of garden design in Japan.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Temple gardens were decorated with large rocks and other raw materials to build [[:en:Japanese dry garden|Karesansui]] or Zen rock gardens. "Their designs imbued the gardens with a sense of the surreal and beckoned viewers to forget themselves and become immersed in the seas of gravel and the forests of moss. By loosening the rigid sense of perception, the actual scales of the garden became irrelevant and the viewers were able to then perceive the huge landscapes deep within themselves."<ref name="Juniper2" />
==== Tea gardens ==== Due to the tea garden’s close relationship with the tea ceremony, "the tea garden became one of the richest expressions of wabi sabi."<ref name="Juniper2" /> These small gardens would usually include many elements of wabi-sabi style design. They were designed in a way that set the scene for the visitor to make their own interpretations and put them in the state of mind in order to participate in the tea ceremony.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Poetry === Japanese poetry such as [[:en:Tanka|Tanka]] and [[:en:Haiku|Haiku]] are very short and focus on the defining attributes of a scene. "By withholding verbose descriptions the poem entices the reader to actively participate in the fulfillment of its meaning and, as with the Zen gardens, to become an active participant in the creative process."<ref name="Juniper2" /> One of the most famous Japanese poets, [[:en:Matsuo Bashō|Basho]], was credited with establishing sabi as definitive emotive force in haiku. Many of his works, as with other wabi-sabi expressions, make no use of sentimentality or superfluous adjectives, only the "devastating imagery of solitude."<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Ceramics === [[File:Hon'ami_Koetsu_Fujisan_1.jpg|thumb|Hon'ami Koetsu Fujisan 1]] As the preference for the more simplistic and modest was on the rise, Zen masters found the ornate ceramics from China less and less attractive and too ostentatious.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Suzuki |first=Nobuo |title=Wabi Sabi: The Wisdom in Imperfection |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2021 |isbn=978-4805316313}}</ref> Potters began to experiment with a more free expression of beauty and strayed away from uniformity and symmetry. New kilns gave potters new colors, forms, and textures, allowing them to create pieces that were unique and nonuniform. These potters used a specific kind of firing which was thought to produce the best ceramics due to the part played by nature and the organic [[:en:ash glaze|ash glaze]]s, a clear embodiment of wabi-sabi.<ref name=":3" />
For example: [[:en:Hon'ami Kōetsu|Hon'ami Kōetsu]]'s (本阿弥 光悦; 1558 – 27 February 1637) white raku bowl called "Mount Fuji" (Shiroraku-Chawan, Fujisan) listed as a national treasure by the Japanese government.<ref name=":3" />
[[:en:Kintsugi|Kintsugi]], a specific technique that uses gold lacquer to repair broken pottery, is considered a wabi-sabi expression.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Flower arrangement === Sen no Rikyu saw the [[:en:Rikka|Rikka]] style that was popular at the time and disliked its adherence to formal rules. He did away with the formalism and the opulent vases from China, using only the simplest vases for the flower displays ([[:en:chabana|chabana]]) in his tea ceremonies.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Instead of using more impressive flowers, he insisted on the use of wildflowers. "[[:en:Ikebana|Ikebana]], like the gardens, uses a living medium in the creative process, and it is this ingredient of life that brings a unique feel to flower arrangements."<ref name="Juniper2" />
Ikebana then became a very important part of the tea ceremony, and the flowers were treated with the utmost respect.<ref name="Juniper2" /> "When a tea-master has arranged a flower to his satisfaction he will place it on the [[tokonoma]], the place of honour in a Japanese room. It rests there like an enthroned prince, and the guests or disciples on entering the room will salute it with a profound bow before making their addresses to the host."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Okakura |first=Kakuzo |title=The Book of Tea |publisher=Applewood Books |year=2008 |isbn=978-0983610601}}</ref>
=== Other examples === {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Honkyoku|Honkyoku]]}} (the traditional {{transliteration|ja|[[shakuhachi]]}} (bamboo flute) music of wandering Zen monks)
A contemporary Japanese exploration of the concept of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} can be found in the influential essay ''[[:en:In Praise of Shadows|In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[:en:Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
Other examples include: * The cultivation of [[:en:Bonsai|Bonsai]] (miniature trees) – a typical bonsai design features wood with a rough texture, pieces of deadwood, and trees with hollow trunks, all intended to highlight the passage of time and nature. Bonsai are often displayed in the autumn or after they have shed leaves for the winter, in order to admire their bare branches. * [[:en:Tea ceremony|Tea ceremony]].<ref name=":022"/>
==Influence upon the West== [[File:Wabi-Sabi Apartment by MAKHNO Studio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concept apartment design and decor]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} has been employed in the Western world in a variety of contexts, including in the arts, technology, media, and mental health, among others.
===The arts=== Many Western designers, writers, poets and artists have utilised {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} ideals within their work to varying degrees, with some considering the concept a key component of their art, and others using it only minimally.
* Designer [[:en:Leonard Koren|Leonard Koren]] (born 1948) published {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-Sabi}} ''for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers'' (1994)<ref name="Koren2"/> as an examination of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite news|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|work=[[:en:The New York Times|The New York Times]]|date=22 September 2010 |access-date=2012-09-25}}</ref> This is the book that first introduced the term "wabi-sabi" into Western aesthetic discourse. * {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concepts historically had extreme importance in the development of Western [[:en:studio pottery|studio pottery]]; [[:en:Bernard Leach|Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques, which is evident in his foundational book ''A Potter's Book''. * The work of American artist [[:en:John Connell (artist)|John Connell]] (1940–2009) is also considered to be centered on the idea of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}};<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref> other artists who have employed the idea include former [[:en:Stuckist|Stuckist]] artist and [[:en:remodernist film|remodernist film]]maker [[:en:Jesse Richards|Jesse Richards]] (born 1975), who employs it in nearly all of his work, along with the concept of {{transliteration|ja|[[mono no aware]]}}. * Some [[:en:haiku in English|haiku in English]] also adopt the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in written style, creating spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[:en:Nick Virgilio|Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[:en:Cor van den Heuvel|Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. {{ISBN|0-671-62837-2}} p285</ref>
===Technology=== During the 1990s, the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[:en:agile programming|agile programming]] and [[:en:wiki|wiki]], used to describe acceptance of the ongoing imperfection of computer programming produced through these methods.<ref>{{cite web|title=Wabi Sabi |url=http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi |access-date=2006-11-19}}</ref>
===Mental health=== Wabi-sabi has been evoked in a mental health context as a helpful concept for reducing [[:en:Perfectionism (psychology)|perfectionist thinking]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.vacounseling.com/wabi-sabi/|title=Wabi Sabi: The Simple Beauty of Serene Melancholy |last=Mathews |first=John |date=February 23, 2016 |website=Virginia Counseling |publisher= |access-date=July 7, 2022 |quote=}}</ref>
===In media=== In 2009, [[:en:Marcel Theroux|Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[:en:BBC Four|BBC Four]], as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming, travelling throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people. Theroux began by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living'' {{transliteration|ja|Wabi Sabi}} by [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]], asking members of the public on a street in Tokyo to describe {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} – the results of which showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable."<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), p. 6.</ref>

It was built during the [[:en:Higashiyama period|Higashiyama period]]. The [[:en:Clay|Clay]] wall, which is stained by age with subtle brown and orange tones, reflects {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} principles, with the rock garden reflecting {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} principles.<ref>森神逍遥 『侘び然び幽玄のこころ』桜の花出版、2015th year Morigami Shouyo,"Wabi sabi yugen no kokoro : seiyo tetsugaku o koeru joi ishiki" (Japanese) {{ISBN|978-4-434-20142-4}}</ref>]] [[File:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|A Japanese tea house which reflects the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in {{nihongo|[[:en:Kenroku-en|Kenroku-en]]|兼六園}} Garden]] [[File:Black Raku tea bowl Amadera.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} tea bowl, [[:en:Azuchi–Momoyama period|Azuchi–Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
In traditional [[:en:Japanese aesthetics|Japanese aesthetics]], {{nihongo||侘び寂び|'''wabi-sabi'''}} is centered on the acceptance of and imperfection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Wabi-Sabi? |url=https://nobleharbor.com/tea/chado/WhatIsWabi-Sabi.htm |access-date=2017-07-13 |website=nobleharbor.com}}</ref> The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of appreciating beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete" in nature.<ref name="Koren2">{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> It is prevalent in many forms of Japanese art.<ref>{{Cite book |last=DAVIES |first=TREVOR |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/1032029879 |title=1001 IDEAS THAT CHANGED THE WAY WE THINK. |date=2018 |publisher=CASSELL ILLUSTRATED |isbn=978-1-78840-088-6 |location=[Place of publication not identified] |pages=293 |oclc=1032029879}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Zia |first=East Liberty |title=Wabi-Sabi: The Japanese Art of Finding the Beauty in Imperfections |url=https://www.carnegielibrary.org/staff-picks/wabi-sabi-the-japanese-art-of-finding-the-beauty-in-imperfections/ |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is a composite of two interrelated aesthetic concepts, {{nihongo|||wabi}} and {{nihongo|||sabi}}. According to the [[:en:Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]], {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be translated as "subdued, austere beauty," while {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} means "rustic [[:en:patina|patina]]."<ref>{{cite web |title=Japanese Aesthetics |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/japanese-aesthetics/ |accessdate=31 October 2022 |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is derived from the [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[:en:Three marks of existence|Three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, {{nihongo|[[:en:Dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[:en:Śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.<ref>Daisetz Suzuki "Zen and Japanese Culture" Iwanami Shoten, 1940 ISBN 978-4004000204 The stillness of the tea ceremony is wider than silence. Synonymous with awabi. (136 pages)</ref>
Characteristics of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetics and principles include [[:en:asymmetry|asymmetry]], roughness, [[:en:simplicity|simplicity]], economy, austerity, modesty, [[:en:intimacy|intimacy]], and the appreciation of both natural objects and the forces of nature.
==Description== {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can be described as "the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of what we think of as traditional Japanese beauty. It occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese of aesthetic values as do the [[:en:Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[:en:Beauty|Beauty]] and perfection in the West."<ref name="Koren2" /> Another description of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} by Andrew Juniper notes that, "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}."<ref name="Juniper2">{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |url=https://archive.org/details/wabisabijapanese00juni |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2003 |isbn=0-8048-3482-2 |url-access=registration}}</ref> For Richard Powell, "{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name="Powell2">{{cite book |author=Powell, Richard R. |title=Wabi Sabi Simple |publisher=Adams Media |year=2004 |isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
When it comes to thinking about an English definition or translation of the words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' Andrew Juniper explains that, "They have been used to express a vast range of ideas and emotions, and so their meanings are more open to personal interpretation than almost any other word in the Japanese vocabulary." Therefore, an attempt to directly translate ''wabi-sabi'' may take away from the ambiguity that is so important to understanding how the Japanese view it.<ref name="Juniper2" />
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} changed to be more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Satori|Satori]]}} or [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. In today's Japan, the meaning of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity". In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty".<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), pp. 20–21.</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} artworks often emphasize the process of making the piece and that it is ultimately incomplete.<ref name=":022">{{Cite journal |last=John |first=Joseph D. |date=2007 |title=Experience as Medium: John Dewey and a Traditional Japanese Aesthetic |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/224026 |journal=The Journal of Speculative Philosophy |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.2307/25670649 |issn=1527-9383 |jstor=25670649}}</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; in this instance, {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or the limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word {{nihongo3|{{lit|to rust}}|錆|sabi}}. Although the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] characters for "rust" are not the same as {{nihongo||寂|sabi}} in {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, the original spoken word (pre-kanji, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yamato-kotoba|Yamato-kotoba]]}}) are believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題, 井上勝也, 裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary_wabi-sabi_tea_bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} style]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[:en:Mahayana Buddhist|Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[:en:Transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Since Mahayana philosophy predicates that genuine understanding is reached through experience rather than words, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} may best be appreciated non-verbally.
Although the {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} concepts are religious in origin, actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual, in keeping with the [[:en:Syncretic|Syncretic]] nature of [[:en:Religion in Japan|Japanese belief]].
==Education== {{Essay-like|section|date=March 2024}} In one sense {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is a training whereby the student of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can change the student's perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.<ref>Yury Lobo, ''In the Wake of Basho: Bestiary in the Rock Garden'', Xlibris, 2017, 23*</ref>
[[File:Meimeian08n4592.jpg|thumb|Nijiriguchi entrance of a tea house]]
== History == Wabi-sabi has roots in ancient Chinese [[Taoism]] and [[:en:Zen|Zen]] Buddhism. It started to shape Japanese culture when the Zen priest [[:en:Murata Jukō|Murata Jukō]] (村田珠光, 1423–1502) modified the [[:en:Japanese tea ceremony|tea ceremony]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Reibstein |first=Mark |title=Wabi Sabi |publisher=Little, Brown |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-316-11825-5 |language=English}}</ref> He introduced simple, rough, wooden and clay instruments to replace the gold, jade, and porcelain of the Chinese style tea service that was popular at the time. About one hundred years later, the tea master [[:en:Sen no Rikyū|Sen no Rikyū]] (千利休, 1522 – April 21, 1591) introduced wabi-sabi to the royalty with his design of the [[:en:Chashitsu|teahouse]]. "He constructed a teahouse with a door so low that even the emperor would have to bow in order to enter, reminding everyone of the importance of humility before tradition, mystery, and spirit."<ref name=":1" />
== In Japanese arts == At first, something that exhibited wabi-sabi qualities could only be discovered; it could be "found in the simple dwellings of the farmers that dotted the landscape, epitomized in neglected stone lanterns overgrown with moss or in simple bowls and other household utensils used by the common folk."<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Teiji |first=Itoh |title=Wabi Sabi Suki: The Essence of Japanese Beauty |publisher=Mazda Motor Corporation |year=1993}}</ref> However, towards the end of the late medieval period, the ruling class began using these aesthetic values to intentionally create "tea ceremony utensils, handicrafts, tea ceremony rooms and cottages, homes, gardens, even food and sweets, and above all manners and etiquette."<ref name=":2" />
Many forms of [[:en:Japanese art|Japanese art]] have been influenced by Zen and Mahayana philosophy over the past thousand years, with the concepts of the acceptance and contemplation of imperfection, and constant [[:en:flux|flux]] and [[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]] of all things being particularly important to Japanese arts and [[:en:Culture of Japan|culture]].<ref name="Juniper2" /> Accordingly, many Japanese art forms can be seen to encapsulate and exemplify the ideals of ''wabi-sabi''.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Garden design === [[File:Kare-sansui zen garden, Ryōan-ji, Kyoto 20190416 1.jpg|thumb|Ryōan-ji (late 16th century) in Kyoto, Japan, a famous example of a Zen garden]] [[:en:Japanese garden|Japanese garden]]s started out as very simple open spaces that were meant to encourage kami, or spirits, to visit. During the Kamakura period Zen ideals began to influence the art of garden design in Japan.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Temple gardens were decorated with large rocks and other raw materials to build [[:en:Japanese dry garden|Karesansui]] or Zen rock gardens. "Their designs imbued the gardens with a sense of the surreal and beckoned viewers to forget themselves and become immersed in the seas of gravel and the forests of moss. By loosening the rigid sense of perception, the actual scales of the garden became irrelevant and the viewers were able to then perceive the huge landscapes deep within themselves."<ref name="Juniper2" />
==== Tea gardens ==== Due to the tea garden’s close relationship with the tea ceremony, "the tea garden became one of the richest expressions of wabi sabi."<ref name="Juniper2" /> These small gardens would usually include many elements of wabi-sabi style design. They were designed in a way that set the scene for the visitor to make their own interpretations and put them in the state of mind in order to participate in the tea ceremony.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Poetry === Japanese poetry such as [[:en:Tanka|Tanka]] and [[:en:Haiku|Haiku]] are very short and focus on the defining attributes of a scene. "By withholding verbose descriptions the poem entices the reader to actively participate in the fulfillment of its meaning and, as with the Zen gardens, to become an active participant in the creative process."<ref name="Juniper2" /> One of the most famous Japanese poets, [[:en:Matsuo Bashō|Basho]], was credited with establishing sabi as definitive emotive force in haiku. Many of his works, as with other wabi-sabi expressions, make no use of sentimentality or superfluous adjectives, only the "devastating imagery of solitude."<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Ceramics === [[File:Hon'ami_Koetsu_Fujisan_1.jpg|thumb|Hon'ami Koetsu Fujisan 1]] As the preference for the more simplistic and modest was on the rise, Zen masters found the ornate ceramics from China less and less attractive and too ostentatious.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Suzuki |first=Nobuo |title=Wabi Sabi: The Wisdom in Imperfection |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2021 |isbn=978-4805316313}}</ref> Potters began to experiment with a more free expression of beauty and strayed away from uniformity and symmetry. New kilns gave potters new colors, forms, and textures, allowing them to create pieces that were unique and nonuniform. These potters used a specific kind of firing which was thought to produce the best ceramics due to the part played by nature and the organic [[:en:ash glaze|ash glaze]]s, a clear embodiment of wabi-sabi.<ref name=":3" />
For example: [[:en:Hon'ami Kōetsu|Hon'ami Kōetsu]]'s (本阿弥 光悦; 1558 – 27 February 1637) white raku bowl called "Mount Fuji" (Shiroraku-Chawan, Fujisan) listed as a national treasure by the Japanese government.<ref name=":3" />
[[:en:Kintsugi|Kintsugi]], a specific technique that uses gold lacquer to repair broken pottery, is considered a wabi-sabi expression.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Flower arrangement === Sen no Rikyu saw the [[:en:Rikka|Rikka]] style that was popular at the time and disliked its adherence to formal rules. He did away with the formalism and the opulent vases from China, using only the simplest vases for the flower displays ([[:en:chabana|chabana]]) in his tea ceremonies.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Instead of using more impressive flowers, he insisted on the use of wildflowers. "[[:en:Ikebana|Ikebana]], like the gardens, uses a living medium in the creative process, and it is this ingredient of life that brings a unique feel to flower arrangements."<ref name="Juniper2" />
Ikebana then became a very important part of the tea ceremony, and the flowers were treated with the utmost respect.<ref name="Juniper2" /> "When a tea-master has arranged a flower to his satisfaction he will place it on the [[tokonoma]], the place of honour in a Japanese room. It rests there like an enthroned prince, and the guests or disciples on entering the room will salute it with a profound bow before making their addresses to the host."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Okakura |first=Kakuzo |title=The Book of Tea |publisher=Applewood Books |year=2008 |isbn=978-0983610601}}</ref>
=== Other examples === {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Honkyoku|Honkyoku]]}} (the traditional {{transliteration|ja|[[shakuhachi]]}} (bamboo flute) music of wandering Zen monks)
A contemporary Japanese exploration of the concept of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} can be found in the influential essay ''[[:en:In Praise of Shadows|In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[:en:Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
Other examples include: * The cultivation of [[:en:Bonsai|Bonsai]] (miniature trees) – a typical bonsai design features wood with a rough texture, pieces of deadwood, and trees with hollow trunks, all intended to highlight the passage of time and nature. Bonsai are often displayed in the autumn or after they have shed leaves for the winter, in order to admire their bare branches. * [[:en:Tea ceremony|Tea ceremony]].<ref name=":022"/>
==Influence upon the West== [[File:Wabi-Sabi Apartment by MAKHNO Studio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concept apartment design and decor]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} has been employed in the Western world in a variety of contexts, including in the arts, technology, media, and mental health, among others.
===The arts=== Many Western designers, writers, poets and artists have utilised {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} ideals within their work to varying degrees, with some considering the concept a key component of their art, and others using it only minimally.
* Designer [[:en:Leonard Koren|Leonard Koren]] (born 1948) published {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-Sabi}} ''for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers'' (1994)<ref name="Koren2"/> as an examination of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite news|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|work=[[:en:The New York Times|The New York Times]]|date=22 September 2010 |access-date=2012-09-25}}</ref> This is the book that first introduced the term "wabi-sabi" into Western aesthetic discourse. * {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concepts historically had extreme importance in the development of Western [[:en:studio pottery|studio pottery]]; [[:en:Bernard Leach|Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques, which is evident in his foundational book ''A Potter's Book''. * The work of American artist [[:en:John Connell (artist)|John Connell]] (1940–2009) is also considered to be centered on the idea of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}};<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref> other artists who have employed the idea include former [[:en:Stuckist|Stuckist]] artist and [[:en:remodernist film|remodernist film]]maker [[:en:Jesse Richards|Jesse Richards]] (born 1975), who employs it in nearly all of his work, along with the concept of {{transliteration|ja|[[mono no aware]]}}. * Some [[:en:haiku in English|haiku in English]] also adopt the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in written style, creating spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[:en:Nick Virgilio|Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[:en:Cor van den Heuvel|Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. {{ISBN|0-671-62837-2}} p285</ref>
===Technology=== During the 1990s, the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[:en:agile programming|agile programming]] and [[:en:wiki|wiki]], used to describe acceptance of the ongoing imperfection of computer programming produced through these methods.<ref>{{cite web|title=Wabi Sabi |url=http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi |access-date=2006-11-19}}</ref>
===Mental health=== Wabi-sabi has been evoked in a mental health context as a helpful concept for reducing [[:en:Perfectionism (psychology)|perfectionist thinking]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.vacounseling.com/wabi-sabi/|title=Wabi Sabi: The Simple Beauty of Serene Melancholy |last=Mathews |first=John |date=February 23, 2016 |website=Virginia Counseling |publisher= |access-date=July 7, 2022 |quote=}}</ref>
===In media=== In 2009, [[:en:Marcel Theroux|Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[:en:BBC Four|BBC Four]], as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming, travelling throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people. Theroux began by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living'' {{transliteration|ja|Wabi Sabi}} by [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]], asking members of the public on a street in Tokyo to describe {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} – the results of which showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable."<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), p. 6.</ref>

It was built during the [[:en:Higashiyama period|Higashiyama period]]. The [[:en:Clay|Clay]] wall, which is stained by age with subtle brown and orange tones, reflects {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} principles, with the rock garden reflecting {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} principles.<ref>森神逍遥 『侘び然び幽玄のこころ』桜の花出版、2015th year Morigami Shouyo,"Wabi sabi yugen no kokoro : seiyo tetsugaku o koeru joi ishiki" (Japanese) {{ISBN|978-4-434-20142-4}}</ref>]] [[File:2002 kenrokuen hanami 0123.jpg|thumb|A Japanese tea house which reflects the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in {{nihongo|[[:en:Kenroku-en|Kenroku-en]]|兼六園}} Garden]] [[File:Black Raku tea bowl Amadera.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} tea bowl, [[:en:Azuchi–Momoyama period|Azuchi–Momoyama period]], 16th century]]
In traditional [[:en:Japanese aesthetics|Japanese aesthetics]], {{nihongo||侘び寂び|'''wabi-sabi'''}} is centered on the acceptance of and imperfection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Wabi-Sabi? |url=https://nobleharbor.com/tea/chado/WhatIsWabi-Sabi.htm |access-date=2017-07-13 |website=nobleharbor.com}}</ref> The aesthetic is sometimes described as one of appreciating beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete" in nature.<ref name="Koren2">{{cite book |last=Koren |first=Leonard |title=Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets and Philosophers |publisher=Stone Bridge Press |year=1994 |isbn=1-880656-12-4}}</ref> It is prevalent in many forms of Japanese art.<ref>{{Cite book |last=DAVIES |first=TREVOR |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/1032029879 |title=1001 IDEAS THAT CHANGED THE WAY WE THINK. |date=2018 |publisher=CASSELL ILLUSTRATED |isbn=978-1-78840-088-6 |location=[Place of publication not identified] |pages=293 |oclc=1032029879}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Zia |first=East Liberty |title=Wabi-Sabi: The Japanese Art of Finding the Beauty in Imperfections |url=https://www.carnegielibrary.org/staff-picks/wabi-sabi-the-japanese-art-of-finding-the-beauty-in-imperfections/ |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is a composite of two interrelated aesthetic concepts, {{nihongo|||wabi}} and {{nihongo|||sabi}}. According to the [[:en:Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]], {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be translated as "subdued, austere beauty," while {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} means "rustic [[:en:patina|patina]]."<ref>{{cite web |title=Japanese Aesthetics |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/japanese-aesthetics/ |accessdate=31 October 2022 |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} is derived from the [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] teaching of the {{nihongo|[[:en:Three marks of existence|Three marks of existence]]|三法印|sanbōin}}, specifically {{nihongo|[[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]]|無常|mujō}}, {{nihongo|[[:en:Dukkha|suffering]]|苦|ku}} and {{nihongo|[[:en:Śūnyatā|emptiness or absence of self-nature]]|空|kū}}.<ref>Daisetz Suzuki "Zen and Japanese Culture" Iwanami Shoten, 1940 ISBN 978-4004000204 The stillness of the tea ceremony is wider than silence. Synonymous with awabi. (136 pages)</ref>
Characteristics of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetics and principles include [[:en:asymmetry|asymmetry]], roughness, [[:en:simplicity|simplicity]], economy, austerity, modesty, [[:en:intimacy|intimacy]], and the appreciation of both natural objects and the forces of nature.
==Description== {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can be described as "the most conspicuous and characteristic feature of what we think of as traditional Japanese beauty. It occupies roughly the same position in the Japanese of aesthetic values as do the [[:en:Ancient Greece|Greek]] ideals of [[:en:Beauty|Beauty]] and perfection in the West."<ref name="Koren2" /> Another description of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} by Andrew Juniper notes that, "If an object or expression can bring about, within us, a sense of serene melancholy and a spiritual longing, then that object could be said to be {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}."<ref name="Juniper2">{{cite book |last=Juniper |first=Andrew |url=https://archive.org/details/wabisabijapanese00juni |title=Wabi Sabi: The Japanese Art of Impermanence |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2003 |isbn=0-8048-3482-2 |url-access=registration}}</ref> For Richard Powell, "{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} nurtures all that is authentic by acknowledging three simple realities: nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect."<ref name="Powell2">{{cite book |author=Powell, Richard R. |title=Wabi Sabi Simple |publisher=Adams Media |year=2004 |isbn=1-59337-178-0}}</ref>
When it comes to thinking about an English definition or translation of the words ''wabi'' and ''sabi'' Andrew Juniper explains that, "They have been used to express a vast range of ideas and emotions, and so their meanings are more open to personal interpretation than almost any other word in the Japanese vocabulary." Therefore, an attempt to directly translate ''wabi-sabi'' may take away from the ambiguity that is so important to understanding how the Japanese view it.<ref name="Juniper2" />
After centuries of incorporating artistic and Buddhist influences from China, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} eventually evolved into a distinctly Japanese ideal. Over time, the meanings of {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} changed to be more lighthearted and hopeful. Around 700 years ago, particularly among the Japanese nobility, understanding emptiness and imperfection was honored as tantamount to the first step to {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Satori|Satori]]}} or [[:en:Enlightenment in Buddhism|enlightenment]]. In today's Japan, the meaning of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is often condensed to "wisdom in natural simplicity". In art books, it is typically defined as "flawed beauty".<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), pp. 20–21.</ref> {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} artworks often emphasize the process of making the piece and that it is ultimately incomplete.<ref name=":022">{{Cite journal |last=John |first=Joseph D. |date=2007 |title=Experience as Medium: John Dewey and a Traditional Japanese Aesthetic |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/224026 |journal=The Journal of Speculative Philosophy |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.2307/25670649 |issn=1527-9383 |jstor=25670649}}</ref>
From an engineering or design point of view, {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} may be interpreted as the imperfect quality of any object, due to inevitable limitations in design and construction/manufacture especially with respect to unpredictable or changing usage conditions; in this instance, {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} could be interpreted as the aspect of imperfect reliability, or the limited mortality of any object, hence the phonological and etymological connection with the Japanese word {{nihongo3|{{lit|to rust}}|錆|sabi}}. Although the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] characters for "rust" are not the same as {{nihongo||寂|sabi}} in {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, the original spoken word (pre-kanji, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yamato-kotoba|Yamato-kotoba]]}}) are believed to be one and the same.<ref>錆びをめぐる話題, 井上勝也, 裳華房, 1994</ref><ref>[http://www2.memenet.or.jp/kinugawa/sabi/00121.htm さびの文字] on the Kinugawa Chain Mfg. Co. Ltd website</ref> [[File:Contemporary_wabi-sabi_tea_bowl.jpg|left|thumb|Modern tea vessel made in the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} style]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} both suggest sentiments of desolation and solitude. In the [[:en:Mahayana Buddhist|Mahayana Buddhist]] view of the universe, these may be viewed as positive characteristics, representing liberation from a material world and [[:en:Transcendence (philosophy)|transcendence]] to a simpler life. Since Mahayana philosophy predicates that genuine understanding is reached through experience rather than words, {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} may best be appreciated non-verbally.
Although the {{transliteration|ja|wabi}} and {{transliteration|ja|sabi}} concepts are religious in origin, actual usage of the words in Japanese is often quite casual, in keeping with the [[:en:Syncretic|Syncretic]] nature of [[:en:Religion in Japan|Japanese belief]].
==Education== {{Essay-like|section|date=March 2024}} In one sense {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} is a training whereby the student of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} learns to find the most basic, natural objects interesting, fascinating and beautiful. Fading autumn leaves would be an example. {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} can change the student's perception of the world to the extent that a chip or crack in a vase makes it more interesting and gives the object greater meditative value. Similarly materials that age such as bare wood, paper and fabric become more interesting as they exhibit changes that can be observed over time.<ref>Yury Lobo, ''In the Wake of Basho: Bestiary in the Rock Garden'', Xlibris, 2017, 23*</ref>
[[File:Meimeian08n4592.jpg|thumb|Nijiriguchi entrance of a tea house]]
== History == Wabi-sabi has roots in ancient Chinese [[Taoism]] and [[:en:Zen|Zen]] Buddhism. It started to shape Japanese culture when the Zen priest [[:en:Murata Jukō|Murata Jukō]] (村田珠光, 1423–1502) modified the [[:en:Japanese tea ceremony|tea ceremony]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Reibstein |first=Mark |title=Wabi Sabi |publisher=Little, Brown |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-316-11825-5 |language=English}}</ref> He introduced simple, rough, wooden and clay instruments to replace the gold, jade, and porcelain of the Chinese style tea service that was popular at the time. About one hundred years later, the tea master [[:en:Sen no Rikyū|Sen no Rikyū]] (千利休, 1522 – April 21, 1591) introduced wabi-sabi to the royalty with his design of the [[:en:Chashitsu|teahouse]]. "He constructed a teahouse with a door so low that even the emperor would have to bow in order to enter, reminding everyone of the importance of humility before tradition, mystery, and spirit."<ref name=":1" />
== In Japanese arts == At first, something that exhibited wabi-sabi qualities could only be discovered; it could be "found in the simple dwellings of the farmers that dotted the landscape, epitomized in neglected stone lanterns overgrown with moss or in simple bowls and other household utensils used by the common folk."<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Teiji |first=Itoh |title=Wabi Sabi Suki: The Essence of Japanese Beauty |publisher=Mazda Motor Corporation |year=1993}}</ref> However, towards the end of the late medieval period, the ruling class began using these aesthetic values to intentionally create "tea ceremony utensils, handicrafts, tea ceremony rooms and cottages, homes, gardens, even food and sweets, and above all manners and etiquette."<ref name=":2" />
Many forms of [[:en:Japanese art|Japanese art]] have been influenced by Zen and Mahayana philosophy over the past thousand years, with the concepts of the acceptance and contemplation of imperfection, and constant [[:en:flux|flux]] and [[:en:Impermanence|Impermanence]] of all things being particularly important to Japanese arts and [[:en:Culture of Japan|culture]].<ref name="Juniper2" /> Accordingly, many Japanese art forms can be seen to encapsulate and exemplify the ideals of ''wabi-sabi''.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Garden design === [[File:Kare-sansui zen garden, Ryōan-ji, Kyoto 20190416 1.jpg|thumb|Ryōan-ji (late 16th century) in Kyoto, Japan, a famous example of a Zen garden]] [[:en:Japanese garden|Japanese garden]]s started out as very simple open spaces that were meant to encourage kami, or spirits, to visit. During the Kamakura period Zen ideals began to influence the art of garden design in Japan.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Temple gardens were decorated with large rocks and other raw materials to build [[:en:Japanese dry garden|Karesansui]] or Zen rock gardens. "Their designs imbued the gardens with a sense of the surreal and beckoned viewers to forget themselves and become immersed in the seas of gravel and the forests of moss. By loosening the rigid sense of perception, the actual scales of the garden became irrelevant and the viewers were able to then perceive the huge landscapes deep within themselves."<ref name="Juniper2" />
==== Tea gardens ==== Due to the tea garden’s close relationship with the tea ceremony, "the tea garden became one of the richest expressions of wabi sabi."<ref name="Juniper2" /> These small gardens would usually include many elements of wabi-sabi style design. They were designed in a way that set the scene for the visitor to make their own interpretations and put them in the state of mind in order to participate in the tea ceremony.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Poetry === Japanese poetry such as [[:en:Tanka|Tanka]] and [[:en:Haiku|Haiku]] are very short and focus on the defining attributes of a scene. "By withholding verbose descriptions the poem entices the reader to actively participate in the fulfillment of its meaning and, as with the Zen gardens, to become an active participant in the creative process."<ref name="Juniper2" /> One of the most famous Japanese poets, [[:en:Matsuo Bashō|Basho]], was credited with establishing sabi as definitive emotive force in haiku. Many of his works, as with other wabi-sabi expressions, make no use of sentimentality or superfluous adjectives, only the "devastating imagery of solitude."<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Ceramics === [[File:Hon'ami_Koetsu_Fujisan_1.jpg|thumb|Hon'ami Koetsu Fujisan 1]] As the preference for the more simplistic and modest was on the rise, Zen masters found the ornate ceramics from China less and less attractive and too ostentatious.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Suzuki |first=Nobuo |title=Wabi Sabi: The Wisdom in Imperfection |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |year=2021 |isbn=978-4805316313}}</ref> Potters began to experiment with a more free expression of beauty and strayed away from uniformity and symmetry. New kilns gave potters new colors, forms, and textures, allowing them to create pieces that were unique and nonuniform. These potters used a specific kind of firing which was thought to produce the best ceramics due to the part played by nature and the organic [[:en:ash glaze|ash glaze]]s, a clear embodiment of wabi-sabi.<ref name=":3" />
For example: [[:en:Hon'ami Kōetsu|Hon'ami Kōetsu]]'s (本阿弥 光悦; 1558 – 27 February 1637) white raku bowl called "Mount Fuji" (Shiroraku-Chawan, Fujisan) listed as a national treasure by the Japanese government.<ref name=":3" />
[[:en:Kintsugi|Kintsugi]], a specific technique that uses gold lacquer to repair broken pottery, is considered a wabi-sabi expression.<ref name="Juniper2" />
=== Flower arrangement === Sen no Rikyu saw the [[:en:Rikka|Rikka]] style that was popular at the time and disliked its adherence to formal rules. He did away with the formalism and the opulent vases from China, using only the simplest vases for the flower displays ([[:en:chabana|chabana]]) in his tea ceremonies.<ref name="Juniper2" /> Instead of using more impressive flowers, he insisted on the use of wildflowers. "[[:en:Ikebana|Ikebana]], like the gardens, uses a living medium in the creative process, and it is this ingredient of life that brings a unique feel to flower arrangements."<ref name="Juniper2" />
Ikebana then became a very important part of the tea ceremony, and the flowers were treated with the utmost respect.<ref name="Juniper2" /> "When a tea-master has arranged a flower to his satisfaction he will place it on the [[tokonoma]], the place of honour in a Japanese room. It rests there like an enthroned prince, and the guests or disciples on entering the room will salute it with a profound bow before making their addresses to the host."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Okakura |first=Kakuzo |title=The Book of Tea |publisher=Applewood Books |year=2008 |isbn=978-0983610601}}</ref>
=== Other examples === {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Honkyoku|Honkyoku]]}} (the traditional {{transliteration|ja|[[shakuhachi]]}} (bamboo flute) music of wandering Zen monks)
A contemporary Japanese exploration of the concept of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} can be found in the influential essay ''[[:en:In Praise of Shadows|In Praise of Shadows]]'' by [[:en:Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|Jun'ichirō Tanizaki]].
Other examples include: * The cultivation of [[:en:Bonsai|Bonsai]] (miniature trees) – a typical bonsai design features wood with a rough texture, pieces of deadwood, and trees with hollow trunks, all intended to highlight the passage of time and nature. Bonsai are often displayed in the autumn or after they have shed leaves for the winter, in order to admire their bare branches. * [[:en:Tea ceremony|Tea ceremony]].<ref name=":022"/>
==Influence upon the West== [[File:Wabi-Sabi Apartment by MAKHNO Studio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concept apartment design and decor]] {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} has been employed in the Western world in a variety of contexts, including in the arts, technology, media, and mental health, among others.
===The arts=== Many Western designers, writers, poets and artists have utilised {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} ideals within their work to varying degrees, with some considering the concept a key component of their art, and others using it only minimally.
* Designer [[:en:Leonard Koren|Leonard Koren]] (born 1948) published {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-Sabi}} ''for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers'' (1994)<ref name="Koren2"/> as an examination of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}}, contrasting it with Western ideals of beauty. According to Penelope Green, Koren's book subsequently "became a talking point for a wasteful culture intent on penitence and a touchstone for designers of all stripes."<ref name=Green>{{cite news|last=Green|first=Penelope|title=An Idiosyncratic Designer, a Serene New Home|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/23/garden/23leonard.html|work=[[:en:The New York Times|The New York Times]]|date=22 September 2010 |access-date=2012-09-25}}</ref> This is the book that first introduced the term "wabi-sabi" into Western aesthetic discourse. * {{transliteration|ja|Wabi-sabi}} concepts historically had extreme importance in the development of Western [[:en:studio pottery|studio pottery]]; [[:en:Bernard Leach|Bernard Leach]] (1887–1979) was deeply influenced by Japanese aesthetics and techniques, which is evident in his foundational book ''A Potter's Book''. * The work of American artist [[:en:John Connell (artist)|John Connell]] (1940–2009) is also considered to be centered on the idea of {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}};<ref>Hess Art Collection, Hatje Cantz, 2010</ref> other artists who have employed the idea include former [[:en:Stuckist|Stuckist]] artist and [[:en:remodernist film|remodernist film]]maker [[:en:Jesse Richards|Jesse Richards]] (born 1975), who employs it in nearly all of his work, along with the concept of {{transliteration|ja|[[mono no aware]]}}. * Some [[:en:haiku in English|haiku in English]] also adopt the {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic in written style, creating spare, minimalist poems that evoke loneliness and transience,{{Citation needed|date=June 2013}} such as [[:en:Nick Virgilio|Nick Virgilio]]'s "autumn twilight:/ the wreath on the door/ lifts in the wind".<ref>[[:en:Cor van den Heuvel|Cor van den Heuvel]], editor. ''The Haiku Anthology''. Fireside, 1986. {{ISBN|0-671-62837-2}} p285</ref>
===Technology=== During the 1990s, the concept was borrowed by computer software developers and employed in [[:en:agile programming|agile programming]] and [[:en:wiki|wiki]], used to describe acceptance of the ongoing imperfection of computer programming produced through these methods.<ref>{{cite web|title=Wabi Sabi |url=http://c2.com/cgi/wiki?WabiSabi |access-date=2006-11-19}}</ref>
===Mental health=== Wabi-sabi has been evoked in a mental health context as a helpful concept for reducing [[:en:Perfectionism (psychology)|perfectionist thinking]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.vacounseling.com/wabi-sabi/|title=Wabi Sabi: The Simple Beauty of Serene Melancholy |last=Mathews |first=John |date=February 23, 2016 |website=Virginia Counseling |publisher= |access-date=July 7, 2022 |quote=}}</ref>
===In media=== In 2009, [[:en:Marcel Theroux|Marcel Theroux]] presented "In Search of Wabi Sabi" on [[:en:BBC Four|BBC Four]], as part of the channel's ''Hidden Japan'' season of programming, travelling throughout Japan trying to understand the aesthetic tastes of its people. Theroux began by comically enacting a challenge from the book ''Living'' {{transliteration|ja|Wabi Sabi}} by [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]], asking members of the public on a street in Tokyo to describe {{transliteration|ja|wabi-sabi}} – the results of which showed that, just as Gold predicted, "they will likely give you a polite shrug and explain that Wabi Sabi is simply unexplainable."<ref>Gold, Taro. (2004) [[:en:Taro Gold|Taro Gold]]'s ''Living Wabi Sabi'' (Kansas City: [[:en:Andrews McMeel Publishing|Andrews McMeel Publishing]], {{ISBN|0-7407-3960-3}}), p. 6.</ref>
